results.name: contains_digit_decade_yes
results.description: Sets of >=2 examples that all contain a digit d but do not all end in d: yes-rate on non-example targets whose tens digit is d and that are >3 from every example; observed above null_mean means people generalise a "contains digit d" rule into the d-decade more than the model's discounted digit rules allow, below means the model over-produces it.
results.code:
# name: contains_digit_decade_yes
# description: Sets of >=2 examples that all contain a digit d but do not all end in d: yes-rate on non-example targets whose tens digit is d and that are >3 from every example; observed above null_mean means people generalise a "contains digit d" rule into the d-decade more than the model's discounted digit rules allow, below means the model over-produces it.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    dig = {}
    for s in sets.unique():
        xs = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")]
        ds = [d for d in range(1, 10) if len(xs) >= 2 and all(str(d) in str(x) for x in xs) and not all(x % 10 == d for x in xs)]
        dig[s] = ds[0] if ds else -1
    d = sets.map(dig).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    ex = sets.str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    m = (d >= 0) & (t // 10 == d) & (t < 100) & (dist > 3)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[m].mean())

results.name: ends5_to_ends0_extension
results.description: Sets of >=2 examples all ending in 5: yes-rate for targets ending in 0 minus targets ending in neither 0 nor 5; observed above null_mean means people read such sets as "multiples of 5" more than the model (which favours "ends in 5"), below means the model over-produces the multiples-of-5 reading.

results.name: item_response_variance
results.description: Mean, over (set, target) items answered >=4 times, of the binomial variance p(1-p) of the item's yes-rate; observed below null_mean means people agree on items more (responses more deterministic/extreme) than the model's intermediate probabilities predict, above means people are less consistent than the model.

results.name: mult3_set_rule_boost
results.description: Sets of >=2 examples that are all multiples of 3 (but not all even): yes-rate for non-example multiple-of-3 targets minus non-example non-multiple-of-3 targets; observed above null_mean means people use the "multiples of 3" rule more than the model predicts, below means the model over-produces it.
results.code:
# name: mult3_set_rule_boost
# description: Sets of >=2 examples that are all multiples of 3 (but not all even): yes-rate for non-example multiple-of-3 targets minus non-example non-multiple-of-3 targets; observed above null_mean means people use the "multiples of 3" rule more than the model predicts, below means the model over-produces it.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = sets.unique()
    ok = {}
    for s in uniq:
        xs = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")]
        ok[s] = len(xs) >= 2 and all(x % 3 == 0 for x in xs) and not all(x % 2 == 0 for x in xs)
    sel = sets.map(ok).values.astype(bool)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    ex = sets.str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    m = sel & ~isex
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a = m & (t % 3 == 0); b = m & (t % 3 != 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: early_vs_late_coincidence_digit_far
results.description: Sets of >=3 examples in which some last digit d is shared by >=2 but not all examples: yes-rate on non-example targets ending in d and >10 from every example when the first two examples share d, minus when the sharing only appears at the 3rd/4th example; observed above null_mean means an early-noticed coincidence drives digit generalisation more than the model's rethink mechanism predicts (order effect too weak), below means the model's order effect is too strong.
results.code:
# name: early_vs_late_coincidence_digit_far
# description: Sets of >=3 examples in which some last digit d is shared by >=2 but not all examples: yes-rate on non-example targets ending in d and >10 from every example when the first two examples share d, minus when the sharing only appears at the 3rd/4th example; observed above null_mean means an early-noticed coincidence drives digit generalisation more than the model's rethink mechanism predicts (order effect too weak), below means the model's order effect is too strong.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    info = {}
    for s in sets.unique():
        xs = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")]
        lab = (-1, -1)
        if len(xs) >= 3:
            ld = [x % 10 for x in xs]
            for d in range(10):
                c = ld.count(d)
                if 2 <= c < len(xs):
                    lab = (d, 1 if (ld[0] == d and ld[1] == d) else 0)
                    break
        info[s] = lab
    lab = sets.map(info)
    d = np.array([v[0] for v in lab.values]); early = np.array([v[1] for v in lab.values])
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    ex = sets.str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    m = (d >= 0) & (t % 10 == d) & (dist > 10)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a = m & (early == 1); b = m & (early == 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: incoherent_wide_set_yes_rate
results.description: Multi-example sets spanning >=50 that no arithmetic or digit rule (odd/even, multiples 3-12, powers, squares, cubes, primes, ends-in/contains digit) fits: yes-rate on non-example targets; observed above null_mean means people generalise rule-less scattered sets more broadly than the model (whose trust/interval mass is too narrow), below means the model over-generalises them.
results.code:
# name: incoherent_wide_set_yes_rate
# description: Multi-example sets spanning >=50 that no arithmetic or digit rule (odd/even, multiples 3-12, powers, squares, cubes, primes, ends-in/contains digit) fits: yes-rate on non-example targets; observed above null_mean means people generalise rule-less scattered sets more broadly than the model (whose trust/interval mass is too narrow), below means the model over-generalises them.
def test_statistic(df):
    N = list(range(1, 101))
    def isprime(n):
        return n > 1 and all(n % a for a in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1))
    rules = [lambda n: n % 2 == 1, lambda n: n % 2 == 0, isprime,
             lambda n: n in {k * k for k in range(1, 11)}, lambda n: n in {1, 8, 27, 64}]
    rules += [(lambda m: (lambda n: n % m == 0))(m) for m in [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12]]
    rules += [(lambda m: (lambda n: n in {m ** k for k in range(1, 8)}))(m) for m in range(2, 11)]
    rules += [(lambda d: (lambda n: n % 10 == d))(d) for d in range(10)]
    rules += [(lambda d: (lambda n: str(d) in str(n)))(d) for d in range(10)]
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    ok = {}
    for s in sets.unique():
        xs = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")]
        ok[s] = len(xs) >= 2 and max(xs) - min(xs) >= 50 and not any(all(f(x) for x in xs) for f in rules)
    sel = sets.map(ok).values.astype(bool)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    ex = sets.str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    m = sel & ~isex
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[m].mean())

results.name: magnitude_scaled_near_extension
results.description: Non-example targets lying outside the examples' [min,max] and 1-10 from the nearest example: yes-rate when that nearest example is >50 minus when it is <=50; observed above null_mean means people extend more generously around large numbers (log-like magnitude similarity) than the model, below means the model's magnitude effect is too strong.
results.code:
# name: magnitude_scaled_near_extension
# description: Non-example targets lying outside the examples' [min,max] and 1-10 from the nearest example: yes-rate when that nearest example is >50 minus when it is <=50; observed above null_mean means people extend more generously around large numbers (log-like magnitude similarity) than the model, below means the model's magnitude effect is too strong.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    ex = sets.str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    diff = np.abs(ex - t[:, None])
    diff = np.where(np.isnan(diff), 1e9, diff)
    j = np.argmin(diff, axis=1)
    dist = diff[np.arange(len(t)), j]
    near = ex[np.arange(len(t)), j]
    out = (t < np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)) | (t > np.nanmax(ex, axis=1))
    m = out & (dist >= 1) & (dist <= 10)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a = m & (near > 50); b = m & (near <= 50)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: mult4_vs_even_specificity
results.description: Sets of >=2 examples that are all multiples of 4: yes-rate for non-example multiple-of-4 targets minus non-example even-but-not-multiple-of-4 targets; observed above null_mean means people pick the more specific "multiples of 4" rule over "even" more sharply than the model (size principle too weak), below means the model is too specific.
results.code:
# name: mult4_vs_even_specificity
# description: Sets of >=2 examples that are all multiples of 4: yes-rate for non-example multiple-of-4 targets minus non-example even-but-not-multiple-of-4 targets; observed above null_mean means people pick the more specific "multiples of 4" rule over "even" more sharply than the model (size principle too weak), below means the model is too specific.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    ok = {}
    for s in sets.unique():
        xs = [int(v) for v in s.split(",")]
        ok[s] = len(xs) >= 2 and all(x % 4 == 0 for x in xs)
    sel = sets.map(ok).values.astype(bool)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    ex = sets.str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    m = sel & ~isex
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a = m & (t % 4 == 0); b = m & (t % 2 == 0) & (t % 4 != 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
